items.title: Bob Stewart interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 24, 2006
items.q: that was my first jazz experience, in McCoy Tyner’s band at the lower east side at Slugs, doing the music from “Tender Moments.”

ctx.x: Did you find that okay you’re playing an instrument that not as many people play perhaps, especially in the jazz world, so there’s not as much competition on your instrument but there’s not as many opportunities? Or did you make your opportunities?

I think both things are probably true. And to one degree or another both things are true at whatever given time. When I first came to New York the only opportunity for tuba was at Your Father’s Moustache, and soon after that, around ’67, McCoy Tyner had recorded an album called “Tender Moments,” all right? With Lee Morgan and James Spaulding, and just some great players. And he was doing some work with that album in New York at Slugs, it was before McCoy was of the stature to be able to go into the Vanguard and…

with being an ensemble horn player in these big band settings. So there were two different positions that I got a chance to be in. And also because of the many hats that I’ve worn I was playing free jazz in Sam Rivers’ Big Band that was performing and working and rehearsing at this time all through the seventies, I was playing Collective Black Artists Big Winds, which was a kind of a cultural, very ethnic — it was swing and everything but it still had a more cultural and ethnic quality to it. Then I was also…
